# Nehemiah 4: Research Notes for a Verse-by-Verse Commentary

**Gaps to know about first:**
- I couldn't open the NET Bible notes, bibleodyssey.org, or any Catholic or Orthodox commentary pages. For those views I only have the Latin Vulgate and Douay translations, as other commentators report them.
- Nothing turned up on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter, so that section is left out.
- Notes on vv. 15–16 and 19–22 are thin.
- The church labels I put on older writers (for example, Clarke and Benson as Methodist) come from my own background knowledge, not from the pages. Please check them before you print them.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Sanballat's reaction grows step by step. He was disturbed in 2:10, scornful in 2:19, and now that work has started he is furious. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/
- Utley: the Hebrew verb for "furious" comes from a word meaning "to burn." The same root is used in a good sense ("zealous") in 3:20. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the Samaritan faction showed their bitter animosity to the Jews on discovering the systematic design of refortifying Jerusalem. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Neh/Neh_004.cfm
- Steven Cole: a strong, independent Jerusalem would weaken Sanballat's control of the region and hurt his trade. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-4-commentary

**v. 2**
- Utley: the word translated "army" can also mean "wealthy men." "Feeble" comes from a verb about withering. Some scholars think "themselves" is a copying error for "God," but no ancient translation reads it that way. "Revive" treats the stones as if they were living things. Burned limestone loses its strength and crumbles to powder. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- Guzik: "Will they offer sacrifices?" sneers that the Jews expect God to build the walls by miracle. Discouraging attacks often hold some truth (the builders really were feeble) but leave out the bigger truth that God is with his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/

**v. 3**
- Foxes in great numbers infested the ruined and desolate places in the mount and city of Zion (Lamentations 5:18). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/nehemiah-4.html
- Utley: Tobiah may have chosen jackals or foxes because they are linked with ruined, cursed cities. His jibe is answered by Kathleen Kenyon's excavation, which found Nehemiah's wall to be nine feet thick. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- Guzik: Tobiah called it "their" wall, but it was really God's wall and God's work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/

**vv. 4–5 (the prayer for judgment)**
- Guzik: For Nehemiah, prayer was a first resource, not a last resort. Praying like this hands one's violent feelings over to God. Guzik says it should never [be] in the sense of praying evil upon them, but in turning them over to a good and just God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/
- Constable: Nehemiah based his prayer on God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:1–3). "Do not forgive" probably refers only to the sin of opposing the builders. Asking for vengeance leaves vengeance to God (Romans 12:19). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-5.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: "cover" means forgive. The enemies openly challenged the wrath of God, by despising Him before the builders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-4.htm
- Cambridge Bible: The people are inseparable from their God; the mockery of Sanballat and Tobiah directed against the Jews affects Jehovah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-4.htm
- Utley: in v. 5 Nehemiah seems to echo Jeremiah 18:23. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- Commentators disagree on whether Christians may pray like this. See section 2.

**v. 6**
- Guzik: God answered the prayer by giving the people "a mind to work." He did it by changing his own people, not the enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/
- Utley: "half" could mean half the height, half the length, or simply "unfinished." "Mind" is literally "heart." https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- Matthew Henry: The reproaches of enemies should quicken us to our duty, not drive us from it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-4.htm

**vv. 7–8**
- Utley: the enemies sat on every side of Judah. Samaria was to the north, the Arabs to the south, Ammon to the east and Ashdod to the west. "Repair" is literally "healing." Attacking would have broken the Persian king's decree, which was politically risky. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- Believer's Study Bible: the enemies' tactics escalate from ridicule to conspiracy to threats. They never actually attacked; they only wore down morale. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-4-commentary
- Guzik: they talked about attacking but didn't do it. They hoped the threat alone would work and create "confusion." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/

**v. 9**
- Chuck Smith: The prayer was not used in lieu of responsible actions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-5.html
- Utley calls it a balance of faith and practicality. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- Guzik: prayer doesn't replace action; it makes our actions effective. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/
- Preacher's Homiletical: There is a time to pray and a time to prepare to fight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/nehemiah-4.html
- Spurgeon expounded vv. 4–5 under the title "The Two Guards Praying and Watching." https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons38.xviii.html

**v. 10**
- Utley: the verse may be a work song the laborers sang. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- Guzik and Cole: the halfway point is when tiredness sets in. The rubbish had to be cleared before building could go on. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-4-commentary
- Spurgeon, in his sermon "Rubbish," applies the verse to sin in the world and in the church. His comfort: if we cannot build, there is One who can. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/rubbish

**v. 11**
- Utley: this is a threat of a surprise attack. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- Guzik: it came just when the workers' spirits were at their lowest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/

**v. 12 (a hard verse to translate)**
- Everyone agrees that "ten times" means "again and again." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-12.htm
- Reading A, a friendly warning. Matthew Henry says these Jews lacked the zeal to help build but were honest enough to report the enemy's plans. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Neh/Neh_004.cfm
- Reading B, "come home." Barnes, Keil & Delitzsch and the Pulpit Commentary think they were urging their own men to leave the work and come home. Keil & Delitzsch explain this as fear for the families left undefended at home. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-12.htm
- Gill goes further: they pretended to be friends, to their brethren, yet seemed to be in friendship with their enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-12.html
- Clarke suggests one Hebrew letter be changed so the verse reads "what they designed against us." But this various reading is not found in any MS., and is not countenanced by any of the versions. https://www.studylight.org/bible/heb/hmd/nehemiah/4-12.html
- Guzik sees God's goodness here: faithful Jews overheard the plot. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/
- Cole sees negativism coming from people who lived near the enemy and weren't involved in the work. https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-4-commentary

**v. 13**
- Bridgeway: Nehemiah still took no risks. He armed all the workers and divided them into two shifts, one working while the other stood guard. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-12.html

**v. 14**
- Matthew Henry: The reigning fear of God is the best antidote against the ensnaring fear of man. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-14.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: this is the God who will fight for them, as in Deuteronomy 3:22 and 20:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-14.htm
- Cambridge Bible: the word for "Lord" here is *Adonai*. For the Jews the struggle was about their survival as a people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-14.htm
- Chuck Smith: remembering the Lord is always the cure for fear. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-14.html
- Utley: God, the "awesome" one, deserves fear, but his enemies do not. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4

**v. 15**
- Gaebelein: Nehemiah saw in it all God's gracious and providential dealings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/nehemiah-4.html
- The Pulpit Commentary, following the scholar Ewald, says no fight happened because the enemy saw the people armed and ready and lost heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-14.htm
- Grant: though being prepared to fight, they were not required to do so. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/nehemiah-4.html

**v. 16**
- Keil & Delitzsch: "my servants" means Nehemiah's personal staff. Each leader stood behind his own people to encourage them and to lead them if attacked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-17.htm

**vv. 17–18**
- Was "one hand" meant literally? Poole and Gill say no: it is a figure of speech meaning ready to work or fight. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-17.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary and Keil & Delitzsch split the workers into two groups. Carriers really did hold a weapon in one hand. Builders needed both hands, so they wore swords at their sides. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-17.htm
- The Cambridge Bible thinks the weapon was probably a light javelin. Keil & Delitzsch disagree. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-17.htm
- Guzik: God's kingdom is built with a sword against spiritual evil and a trowel to build up God's people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/
- Spurgeon named his magazine *The Sword and the Trowel* after this verse. He wrote that it would not bear the Sword in vain, but use it against error. https://www.spurgeon.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/ST-1889-Edited.pdf

**vv. 19–20**
- Matthew Henry: The work was large, and the builders were dispersed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-19.html
- Chuck Smith pictures the trumpet calling everyone to drop their trowels and run to the spot. He links "troublous times" in Daniel 9:25 to this rebuilding. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-19.html
- Preacher's Homiletical, on "our God shall fight for us": Our God—the attestation of experience. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/nehemiah-4.html

**vv. 21–22**
- Preacher's Homiletical: men from outlying towns now had to stay in the city day and night. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/nehemiah-4.html
- Coffman sees this as Nehemiah's answer to the frightened villagers of v. 12. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-12.html

**v. 23 (the hardest clause in the chapter)**
- The Hebrew literally reads something like "each his weapon, the water." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-23.htm
- The KJV has "put them off for washing." Gill explains this as ritual washing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-23.html
- Ellicott thinks it best to read "every man went with his weapon to the water." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-23.htm
- The Cambridge Bible: 'The text is probably faulty.' https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-23.htm
- Clarke prefers a variant in one manuscript. This shows how all interpreters have been puzzled with this vexatious clause. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-23.html
- Preacher's Homiletical: The idea of the whole verse is clear—unceasing watchfulness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/nehemiah-4.html

---

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ: vv. 4–5

The split here runs across church traditions rather than between them.

**Teachers who say Christians should not copy this prayer**
- Spurgeon (Baptist): This was righteous indignation, but Nehemiah is not a perfect model for us. He was not only stern, but he mingled with his severity a measure of bitterness in his prayer that we must not imitate. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons38.xviii.html
- Adam Clarke (Methodist, my label): taken literally, the prayer is not lawful for any Christian. He also suggests it may be a statement of what will happen rather than a request, because the Hebrew verb form allows both. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-4.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-5.html
- Benson (Methodist, my label): Probably they were uttered rather by a spirit of prophecy than a spirit of prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-4.htm
- Matthew Henry (Presbyterian/Nonconformist, my label) agrees: prophecy rather than prayer, not to be imitated by us who are taught of Christ to pray for those that despitefully use and persecute us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-5.html
- Pulpit Commentary (Rawlinson, Anglican, my label): the prayer is no pattern for Christians. It reflects Nehemiah's hot and hasty temperament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-4.htm

**Teachers who defend the prayer as right**
- Poole (Puritan, my label): the requests were both just, as being directed against such malicious, inveterate, and implacable enemies to God and to his people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-4.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the prayer came from zeal for God's glory, not hatred. Coffman agrees. Coffman also says nothing in Nehemiah's prayer ... is not contained embryonically in every prayer of a Christian today. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-5.html
- Gill (Baptist, my label): a prophecy spoken from a public spirit for the glory of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-5.html
- Geneva Study Bible (Reformed): fleeing to God in prayer is the remedy that the children of God have against the derision and threatenings of their enemies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-4.htm

**Calvary Chapel / charismatic-leaning teachers**
- Guzik says such prayers are proper as long as one hands enemies over to God rather than wishing evil on them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-4/
- Chuck Smith frankly admits he relates to Nehemiah more easily than to "Love your enemies." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-5.html

**Lutheran**
- I found only a Luther quotation on prayer as the Church's wall and fortress, cited in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/nehemiah-4.html
- Keil & Delitzsch report that Luther translated v. 23 as "everyone left off washing." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-23.htm

---

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship (as relayed by Utley and the Cambridge Bible)**
- v. 2: the "themselves → God" reading is a scholarly guess recorded in the notes of the standard Hebrew Bible (*Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia*). https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- v. 6: Kenyon's excavation of the wall. https://bible.org/seriespage/nehemiah-4
- v. 23: suggested corrections to the Hebrew, including "each kept his weapon in his hand." That is the reading the RSV and NRSV follow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-23.htm
- The NET Bible's own translation of v. 12 (warnings about "all the schemes they were plotting") shows up in Bible Hub's parallel versions. Its translator notes weren't available. https://biblehub.com/nehemiah/4-12.htm

**Catholic tradition**
- The Vulgate reads v. 23 as "each one stripped only for the bath." The Pulpit Commentary doubts the Hebrew can mean this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/4-23.htm
- Gill notes that the Vulgate's word is "baptism." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/4-23.html
- The Douay-Rheims follows the Vulgate. https://biblehub.com/nehemiah/4-23.htm
